original_question: Let BAD(alpha, beta, gamma; delta) be the set of xi = (theta_1, theta_2, theta_3) in [0,1]^3 such that inf_p max{p^alpha ||p theta_1||, p^beta ||p theta_2||, p^gamma ||p theta_3||} >= delta, and let BAD(alpha, beta, gamma) be the union of these sets over delta > 0, where alpha + beta + gamma = 1. For two distinct triples (alpha_1, beta_1, gamma_1) and (alpha_2, beta_2, gamma_2), is the intersection BAD(alpha_1, beta_1, gamma_1) ∩ BAD(alpha_2, beta_2, gamma_2) nonempty?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in Section 1: the higher-dimensional weighted Schmidt conjecture about intersections of weighted badly approximable sets, together with the nearby reformulation/context in Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the weighted badly approximable condition, uses the right normalization on the weights (α+β+γ=1), and asks the Schmidt-type intersection question for different weight data. Also, your notation BAD(α,β,γ;δ) and the union over δ>0 is equivalent to the usual paper-style definition via the existence of a constant c>0, at least when all weights are strictly positive.
missing_details: The paper formulates the problem in vector notation for arbitrary dimension n, using weight vectors r=(r_1,...,r_n) in R_n := {r_i \ge 0, \sum_i r_i = 1}, not just triples (α,β,γ).
The official formulation is not restricted to two weight vectors or to n=3; it is posed for any finite or countable set W of admissible weight vectors.
The paper's target conclusion is stronger than nonemptiness: it asks for full Hausdorff dimension, namely dim_H(\bigcap_{r\in W} Bad(r)) = n.
The paper allows zero weights r_i=0 and uses the convention ||qy_i||^{1/0} = 0; your draft implicitly excludes this case by requiring α,β,γ>0.
The ambient space in the paper is \mathbb{R}^n (periodicity lets one restrict to [0,1]^n if desired, but that is not the official statement).
The paper defines Bad(r) directly by: there exists c(y)>0 such that max_i ||qy_i||^{1/r_i} \ge c(y) q^{-1} for all q\in\mathbb{N}; it does not package the condition primarily through BAD(r;δ).
The distance symbol ||\cdot|| must be stated explicitly as distance to the nearest integer, and the quantifier is over all positive integers q.
Relative to the paper, your draft captures only a special case of the conjecture rather than the exact official formulation.
refined_question:
Let n\in\mathbb{N}, let \mathcal{R}_n := \{\mathbf r=(r_1,\dots,r_n)\in[0,\infty)^n : r_1+\cdots+r_n=1\}, and for \mathbf r\in\mathcal{R}_n define
Bad(\mathbf r) := \left\{\mathbf y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n : \exists c(\mathbf y)>0\ \text{such that}\ \max_{1\le i\le n} \|qy_i\|^{1/r_i} \ge c(\mathbf y) q^{-1}\ \text{for all}\ q\in\mathbb{N}\right\},
with the convention \|qy_i\|^{1/0}=0. Is it true that for every finite or countable subset W\subset\mathcal{R}_n one has
\dim_H\!\left(\bigcap_{\mathbf r\in W} Bad(\mathbf r)\right)=n?
justification: The draft is a faithful positive-weight, two-weight-vector, n=3 special case of the higher-dimensional weighted Schmidt problem discussed at the start of the paper. However, the nearest official formulation in the paper is Conjecture 1.1 itself: it is stated for arbitrary admissible weight vectors in arbitrary dimension and asks for full Hausdorff dimension of arbitrary finite/countable intersections, not merely nonemptiness of one two-weight intersection in dimension 3. Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 are the nearby results the paper uses to sharpen/frame this conjectural picture in Section 1.
